ACQUIREDFall 2026 · Episode 1Disney, Part II: The Renaissance and the Empire

The Flywheel and the Firehose

In 1984 Disney was worth more dead than alive. Forty years later it runs a dozen theme parks, Pixar, Marvel, Star Wars, ESPN and a streaming service with well over 100 million subscribers. This is a scene-by-scene retelling of how it happened, and of the business lessons Ben Gilbert and David Rosenthal pulled out along the way.

An unofficial, illustrated companion to the episode. Listen at acquired.fm. Paintings are watercolor renderings of freely licensed photographs. Numbers are the hosts' unless marked otherwise.

SceneWho pays the bills
Era1984 → 2026

One question runs through the whole episode

Walt Disney's business model is easy to draw. You make characters people love, in stories no other studio can tell as well. Then you sell those characters again and again: on lunchboxes and dresses, on rides, and in theatrical re-releases timed for each new generation of kids. The hosts call it the flywheel.

The surprise of Part II is how rarely the flywheel paid for itself. In 1984 the films barely broke even. For most of the 2000s, a cable sports channel in Bristol, Connecticut was the real engine. Today it's the theme parks. Step through the eras to see the money move.

Where Disney's profit came from

That is the tension of the episode's title. The flywheel wants a few rare, beloved stories. The businesses that paid the bills (broadcast, cable, and now streaming) want volume. Every CEO in this story had to decide which one to feed.

REEL01
SceneDisney in chaos
Years1966 → 1984

Worth more broken up

Eighteen or so years after Walt's death, the company he built had stopped making the thing everything else depended on. Disney Animation released three features between 1971 and 1984. The Black Cauldron had been in development for nearly a decade. Earnings fell 19% in 1982 and another 7% in 1983, and the stock slid from $82 to $52.

Ben's breakdown of 1984 is the whole problem in one line. Parks and consumer products earned roughly a quarter of a billion dollars. Film and television earned about $2 million. The parks were living off characters created decades earlier, and ticket prices had barely moved since Walt died. Parking at Disneyland still cost a dollar.

Raiders noticed. The board weighed breaking the company up: selling the film library (Snow White, Cinderella, Sleeping Beauty) to MGM and the parks to hotel operators. To fend off hostile bidders, management cut friendly deals with the Bass family of Fort Worth, who ended up with about 25% of the company. Ben calls it hiring a friendly raider to keep out the hostile ones.

Then the insiders moved. Roy E. Disney, Walt's nephew, had quit the company and was plotting against CEO Ron Miller, Walt's son-in-law. With his partner Stanley Gold and the Basses behind him, Roy forced Miller out in a boardroom coup on September 7, 1984.

Lesson 01Reel 1

A stalled content engine starves everything downstream.

Parks, products and re-releases all spend the same asset: new characters people love. Stop making them and the rest of the business quietly runs down.

REEL02
SceneFourteen days, three men
Years1984 → 1989

Singles, doubles and a dollar parking lot

Within two weeks the board had its new team. Frank Wells, a lawyer and former president of Warner Bros., went first, then told the board to call Michael Eisner, the number two to Barry Diller at Paramount. Eisner insisted on the top job. Wells agreed to be president and peacekeeper. On September 21, 1984 they were introduced as CEO and president. Eisner brought Jeffrey Katzenberg from Paramount to run the studio.

Their Paramount playbook was cheap and disciplined: keep budgets low, skip the A-list by default, and bet on the script. Shareholders liked the phrase "singles and doubles." Talent didn't, so they rebranded it "high concept." A Katzenberg memo of the era made the point that a star can open a movie but can't carry it. Stars are for sale. A good story is what the audience actually experiences.

27 of the first 33

Each card is one of the new regime's first 33 live-action films. Filled cards made money; dashed ones lost it. Hover or tap for the hit list.

Down and Out in Beverly Hills, Three Men and a Baby, Good Morning, Vietnam, Dead Poets Society, Pretty Woman: comeback stars, modest budgets, strong concepts.

Source: David's count of the first 33 films. The partnership Silver Screen financed the live-action slate, about 75 films over eight years. Which six lost money isn't specified, so their positions are illustrative.

David's framing: that's 33 venture investments with only six losers, in a business where returns follow a power law. The films were financed off the balance sheet by a partnership called Silver Screen. Stars coming off rehab or a flop were cheap, and Ben compares the approach to Buffett's cigar-butt investing.

Meanwhile the parks had enormous pricing headroom. Ticket and parking prices had sat still for nearly two decades. Raise parking from $1 to $5 and attendance doesn't move, but every extra dollar drops straight to profit. Eisner raised prices and kept raising them.

Lesson 02Reel 2

Bet on the story, not the star.

A famous name can open a film. Only the story makes it last. Disciplined budgets and strong concepts turned the studio into a portfolio with a 27-for-33 record.

Lesson 03Reel 2

Price to the value you already deliver.

The parks had been underpriced for two decades. Raising prices cost no visitors and fell straight to the bottom line, funding everything that came next.

REEL03
SceneThe Renaissance
Years1984 → 1994

Turn the cartoons into Broadway musicals

Animation was the problem nobody in the new regime understood. Ben tells the story of Eisner pointing at the animation building on his first day and asking Katzenberg what they did down there. Neither of them knew. The answer, of course, was that's where the movies that built the company came from.

The animators were moved off the Burbank lot to a rickety building in Glendale. Roy E. Disney took charge of the division, and Peter Schneider, a theater manager, was brought in to run it. Schneider questioned everything, from the paint process to why nobody used computers. Headcount eventually climbed from about 150 to 550.

The creative unlock was structural. Disney's animated features would become Broadway musicals, with a theater song structure. Katzenberg recruited the lyricist Howard Ashman, who brought the composer Alan Menken from their off-Broadway hit Little Shop of Horrors. Ashman's rule was that early in the film the heroine gets an "I want" song. The Little Mermaid (1989) was modest in theaters and enormous on video. Then came Beauty and the Beast, Aladdin and The Lion King.

The cost side mattered as much. In 1990, pushed by Roy, Disney spent about $10 million building CAPS, a computer ink-and-paint and compositing system, with help from a small graphics company called Pixar. It replaced hand painting of cels and worked like a multiplane camera with unlimited planes. The Little Mermaid had three multiplane shots. The Lion King had hundreds. Beauty and the Beast's ballroom blended a 3D-rendered room with hand-drawn dancers.

Budgets stayed flat. Grosses didn't.

Production budget versus worldwide box office for the three Renaissance peaks, drawn to the same scale.

Production budgetBox office

Hosts' figures (Ben): Beauty and the Beast $25M → ~$330M; Aladdin $28M → ~$500M; The Lion King $45M → ~$750M. The Little Mermaid's budget was about $40M (David); its theatrical gross isn't given.

Ashman died of AIDS in 1991, a few years before The Lion King opened. The hosts treat his loss as a real one. The writers and composers were the magic, even though they were neither the executives nor the people who pitched the stories.

Lesson 04Reel 3

Invest in the process, not just the picture.

A $10M production system and a proven song structure held budgets near $25–45M while grosses grew past half a billion. Better craft and lower cost came from the same investment.

REEL04
SceneThe vault opens
Years1985 → 1994

Every new window sells the same story again

Until 1985 there was no way to watch a Disney film outside a theater. Walt's flywheel re-released each classic every seven years or so. Pinocchio had been through five theatrical runs. Then the company put it on VHS: a limited run of 1.7 million cassettes at $29.95. They sold out, bringing in about $50 million for little more than the cost of the tapes.

Home video quickly became a billion-dollar business, second only to the parks. David says he read that Disney kept $17 to $20 per tape thanks to its leverage over retailers. Eisner's observation was that kids break and lose tapes, so families buy them again.

Cassettes sold

VHS units, by title. The Lion King became the best-selling VHS of all time, according to David.

Hosts' figures: Pinocchio (1985) 1.7M at $29.95; Cinderella (next year) 6M alongside a $34M theatrical re-release; Aladdin ~30M (1993); The Lion King ~32M (1995), about $1B in tape sales.

The same logic ran through everything Eisner's team touched. More than 750 Disney Stores opened in malls. Beauty and the Beast went to Broadway, and Disney bought and restored the New Amsterdam Theatre on 42nd Street. The Lion King musical followed. David counts more than $11 billion in lifetime grosses from tours, London and New York, and calls it perhaps the highest-grossing entertainment product ever. Ben pushed back on that.

What one hit was worth

The hosts' back-of-envelope for The Lion King's cash in its first year or so. Click a layer.

Total: about three-quarters of a billion dollars in cash from a film that cost about $45M to make.

David's estimate, adjusted by Ben: ~$250M theatrical cash after distribution and marketing, plus ~$500M from home video at 50%+ margins. Excludes merchandise, parks and the stage show.

The parks became resorts: the Grand Floridian, the Swan and the Dolphin, the Vacation Club timeshares, Hollywood Studios and later Animal Kingdom. Ben's framing is that a day at the park used to compete with a Saturday ball game. Now a Disney World trip competed with a five-day European vacation. Euro Disney was the one real stumble. It cost about $4 billion and lost money for years. David's joke is that it took a decade to learn European parents want wine.

~8×Operating profit, from well under $300M (1984) to just under $2B a decade laterDavid
10×Market cap, to $22B by 1994, the most valuable media companyDavid

Lesson 05Reel 4

Every new window re-sells the same story.

Video, stores, Broadway and resorts each monetized characters that already existed. The cost of the story was paid once; the returns kept coming.

REEL05
SceneEaster Sunday
Years1994 → 1996

The peacekeeper dies

On Easter Sunday 1994, Frank Wells died in a helicopter crash while heli-skiing. David calls him the yin to Eisner's yang. He held operations together, calmed people down and mediated between two very large personalities. About three months later, at the Allen & Company conference in Sun Valley, Eisner had chest pains and was flown to Los Angeles for an emergency quadruple bypass.

The partnership, before and after

Katzenberg believed he'd been promised Wells's job if it ever opened up. Roy E. Disney and others thought he was brilliant at the studio but not ready to run the company. Eisner sat on the decision, so Katzenberg left. With Steven Spielberg and David Geffen he founded DreamWorks, a full-stack rival with an animation studio down the street in Glendale. Its first big hire was Brenda Chapman, head of story on The Lion King. He also sued for bonuses he said he was owed. David says the case settled years later for a reported $280 million.

Eisner made himself president, then hired his friend Michael Ovitz, the co-founder of the talent agency CAA, as number two. Ben's diagnosis is a job-description mismatch. An agent gets liked, says yes and juggles a hundred deals. A president sits in meetings, herds cats and says no. Ovitz left in December 1996, after 14 months, with about $140 million in severance.

Lesson 06Reel 5

The peacekeeper is load-bearing.

Wells's job looked like administration. In practice he was the arbiter between two strong executives. When he died, the partnership that produced the Renaissance came apart within months.

Lesson 07Reel 5

A great dealmaker isn't automatically an operator.

Agents win by saying yes; presidents win by saying no. Hiring for reputation instead of the job cost Disney 14 months and $140 million.

REEL06
SceneThe accidental goldmine
Years1993 → 2011

A $19 billion deal at Sun Valley

In 1993 the FCC repealed the financial-interest and syndication rules, which had barred TV networks from owning the shows they aired. Studios and networks could now combine. Eisner, who started his career at ABC, tried CBS, found NBC wasn't for sale and lowballed ABC. Then, at Sun Valley in 1995, he hoped to bump into Warren Buffett. Buffett called over Tom Murphy, CEO of Capital Cities/ABC, of which Berkshire was the largest shareholder. Within about a week, Disney agreed to buy the company for $19 billion. It was the second-largest acquisition in history to that point, after RJR Nabisco.

The prize turned out to be a cable channel nobody was focused on. ESPN had passed from Getty Oil to Texaco to ABC, with Hearst holding 20%. It pioneered the business model that would fund Disney for twenty years: instead of paying cable operators for carriage, it charged them a monthly fee for every subscriber. Sports rights were its leverage. Drop ESPN in a carriage dispute and your customers lose the game.

The affiliate-fee machine

Annual fees = subscribers × monthly fee × 12. Drag the sliders, or load a scenario.

66M
$0.90

Hosts' figures: ~66M subscribers and an average fee under $1/month in 1995; about $9.42/month today, roughly 4× the next most expensive channel; ~92M subscribers in 2015 after losing ~3M. "Peak bundle" multiplies 2015 subscribers by today's fee to show the scale; it isn't a reported year.

ESPN's habit was to call cable operators every year or two and ask for about 20% more, while locking up sports rights for as long as a decade. In 1998 it added Sunday and Monday Night Football. From 2008 to 2011, cable networks, about three-quarters of them ESPN, produced about 60% of Disney's operating income, more than $5 billion a year.

B

Ben's pointThe deal was clearly worth it, because ESPN was a near-endless source of cash. It also cost Disney its clarity. From then on it ran two business models under one roof, the character flywheel and an advertising-and-affiliate-fee TV business, and it would never again be only Disney.

The firewall worked. ESPN was left to be the best ESPN it could be, and Mickey and SportsCenter never met. Eisner also turned down an approach from AOL's Steve Case before AOL bought Time Warner. The hosts rank that among his best decisions.

Lesson 08Reel 6

Own the supplier every customer must have, and fence it off.

Must-have sports rights let ESPN raise fees for two decades. Keeping it separate from the Disney brand let both businesses do what they did best.

REEL07
SceneSave Disney
Years2001 → 2005

Forty-three percent

After 1994 the animation slate never found another Lion King. Talent left for DreamWorks, and competing offers drove costs up. The decline showed up late in the numbers because the parks and the Renaissance characters cushioned it. Then came September 11, 2001. The parks fell off a cliff, the stock dropped nearly 25%, and most of the 750 Disney Stores closed. The Bass family, Eisner's strongest backers, faced margin calls elsewhere and sold about $2 billion of Disney stock in a block.

On November 30, 2003, Roy E. Disney resigned from the board, as did Stanley Gold. Roy's three-page letter, sent to the board and the major newspapers, listed seven failures. They ranged from ABC's ratings slump and micromanagement to under-investment in the parks, a creative brain drain, a broken relationship with Pixar and no succession plan. He and Gold launched SaveDisney.com, which David calls the first grassroots shareholder campaign of its kind.

March 3, 2004: the annual meeting

Held in Philadelphia, a few blocks from Comcast. Each square is 1% of the vote on Eisner.

Withheld support: ~43%Supported

Hosts' figures. Two major proxy advisers and CalPERS recommended withholding votes. That night the board stripped Eisner of the chairmanship; he stayed CEO. Comcast withdrew its bid weeks later.

Eisner announced he would leave when his contract ran out at the end of 2006, and the board opened a public search. The first draft of the press release said it would consider internal and external candidates. Bob Iger, then COO, asked who the internal candidates were. Told it was only him, he asked to be named in the release.

Iger's problem was that he had been Eisner's number two for years. So, with help from a political consultant, he ran entirely on the future. He set out three pillars: great branded content, embracing technology as both a creative tool and a distribution channel, and global growth, especially in China and India. The board named him CEO in March 2005 and moved Eisner's exit up to September.

B

Ben's rankingESPN is the first, second and third reason Eisner was a great CEO. The Renaissance is the fourth. David adds that the Lion King musical has to count for something.

Lesson 09Reel 7

When you inherit the record, campaign on the future.

As the deputy of an unpopular CEO, Iger couldn't run on the past. He made the succession about three pillars for what came next, and won.

REEL08
ScenePixar
Years1979 → 2006

The studio Disney fired, then bought

John Lasseter worked the Jungle Cruise at Disneyland, studied at CalArts under Disney's veteran animators, and joined Disney Animation in the early 1980s. He pitched The Brave Little Toaster as a computer-animated film. Asked whether that would be faster or cheaper, he said no; it would push storytelling forward. He was let go the same day.

Ed Catmull had studied computer graphics at the University of Utah alongside future founders of Netscape and Adobe. George Lucas hired him in 1979 to build a graphics group at Lucasfilm. Catmull could build the technology but not characters with feeling, so he brought in Lasseter. When Lucas needed cash during his divorce, he sold the group. In 1986 Steve Jobs paid Lucas $5 million and put another $5 million into the new company, Pixar, taking 70% (employees held 30%). It sold a few hundred Pixar Image Computers. Its first big check came from Disney, for CAPS.

Toy Story was green-lit on January 19, 1993, on terms that favored Disney heavily. A disastrous December 1993 story-reel screening shut production down until Pixar rewrote the film in a few weeks. It rendered one to two hours per frame on 117 Sun machines. It opened on November 22, 1995, grossed nearly $400 million worldwide, and was the year's top film. A week later Pixar went public. It raised about $140 million, more than Netscape, at a market cap of about $1.5 billion. Jobs, who had put in about $54 million over nine years, owned 78%, about $1.2 billion.

Then the relationship decayed. Disney wanted to send Toy Story 2 straight to video. It went to theaters instead and grossed almost $500 million. In 2002 Eisner testified to Congress attacking Apple's "Rip. Mix. Burn." campaign. He wrote a memo to his board predicting Finding Nemo would flop and give Pixar a reality check. The memo leaked. The film grossed about $871 million, and the hosts heard its DVD sold some 65 million copies.

Who got the profits

How the split of a Pixar film's profits moved as Pixar's leverage grew. Step through the four deals.

Hosts' characterization of the terms. 1993: Disney funded the ~$30M budget and marketing and owned the characters; Pixar got under 10% of profits. 1996: nominally 50/50, but distribution economics left Disney nearer 65%. 2004: Jobs' final ask was 100% of profits to Pixar for a 10% distribution fee. 2006: Disney buys Pixar for ~$7.4B in stock.

In January 2004 Pixar ended talks and posted a press release on its own website saying Disney would not share in its future. Iger's first call as CEO was to Jobs. Jobs asked how long Iger had worked for Michael, heard "ten years," and said he didn't see how anything would change. Iger's insight came at the opening parade of Hong Kong Disneyland, where every character from the past decade came from Pixar, not Disney. (The hosts place this during his audition; the park opened in September 2005, so treat the timing loosely.)

He asked the board for permission to propose buying Pixar. Ben says the board was so surprised it forgot to say no. The pitch was to keep Pixar intact in Emeryville and have Lasseter and Catmull also run Disney Animation. Iger even offered them the option of declaring it unfixable and shutting it down. They chose to fix it. On the morning of the January 2006 announcement, Jobs walked Iger around the Pixar campus and told him his cancer had returned. Iger had about half an hour to back out and didn't. Jobs became Disney's largest shareholder, with about 7% (Ben) or 7.7% (David), more than the Disney family held.

B

Ben's payback mathStrip out Pixar's cash and the price is about $6.4 billion. The Toy Story franchise alone has returned something like $3.5 billion in high-margin revenue to Disney, from box office and a cut of roughly $30 billion in lifetime retail sales, before counting the parks. That's half to two-thirds of the price from one franchise.

Disney Animation's run after the deal (The Princess and the Frog, Tangled, Frozen, Big Hero 6, Zootopia, Moana) used Pixar's process: story reels iterated until they work, and notes without ego. Kristen Bell told the hosts the studio still works that way.

Lesson 10Reel 8

Don't squeeze your best creative partner.

Eisner treated Pixar as a counterparty to beat, even hoping Nemo would flop for leverage. Pixar answered by proving it could walk, and the price of keeping it went to $7.4 billion.

Lesson 11Reel 8

Buy the culture, then let it fix you.

The Pixar deal was really about Lasseter, Catmull and their process. Putting them in charge of Disney Animation revived the core of the flywheel.

REEL09
SceneA bigger canvas
Years2009 → 2015

Marvel, Lucasfilm, and the channel that paid for them

Marvel cost about $4 billion in 2009. David notes that $4 billion for a comic book company looked contrarian. Marvel had licensed away its best-known characters (the X-Men to Fox, Spider-Man to Sony), but Iron Man had shown its second string could carry a film. The Marvel Cinematic Universe became the blueprint for building out a whole franchise universe. Through 2025 it grossed about $32 billion across 37 films, more than Star Wars or James Bond. Endgame alone made about $2.8 billion.

Lucasfilm followed in 2012, also for about $4 billion. David sees the same thesis as Pixar: give great storytellers a bigger canvas. Ben thinks Star Wars had less untapped room than hoped, though he loves Andor and Rogue One. Meanwhile Frozen (2013) sold 3 million Elsa and Anna dresses in its first year, and Disney-branded retail passed $50 billion a year.

Priced in years of cable profit

Ben's way of sizing the three deals: how many years of Disney's cable-network profit each one cost.

Ben's arithmetic: Pixar ($7.4B, 2006) ≈ 2.5 years; Marvel ($4B, 2009) < 1 year; Lucasfilm ($4B, 2012) < 1 year. About four years of cable profit bought all three. Bars for "under a year" are drawn at ~0.9 years.

B

Ben's pointThis is the Buffett model inside a media company: cash producers funding cash consumers. ESPN's affiliate fees bought the franchise IP. Iger paid more than most would have, mostly in newly issued stock, and shareholders were diluted for it.

$32B→$52BRevenue, Iger's first decade (2005–15)David

Lesson 12Reel 9

Let the cash producer fund the cash consumers.

A steady, unglamorous profit engine (affiliate fees) bought the irreplaceable assets (franchise IP) that would feed the flywheel for decades.

REEL10
SceneAugust 4, 2015
Years2015

"Modest subscriber losses"

On the fiscal third-quarter call of 2015, Iger mentioned that ESPN was seeing modest subscriber losses from cord-cutting. The annual report later showed about 3 million lost that year, leaving roughly 92 million. Disney's stock had hit an all-time high that same day. The next day it fell about 10%. Fox, Time Warner and Discovery fell with it, and Viacom dropped more than 20%.

Since that day

Growth multiple from August 2015 to the recording (mid-2026).

Hosts' figures: Disney's stock is roughly where it was in August 2015; the S&P 500 is about 3.5×. Endpoints only; no path is implied.

The rest of legacy media spent the decade consolidating. Time Warner went to AT&T, then merged with Discovery. Viacom re-merged with CBS and became Paramount, which Skydance bought. Netflix and YouTube took the profits. The hosts say the old studios became something like serfs in the tech companies' streaming kingdoms, with Disney the one exception.

B

Ben's pointMarket cap is the market's estimate of future cash flows. A flat stock since 2015 means investors think Disney's future looks no brighter now than it did on that August day.

Lesson 13Reel 10

The market prices the engine, not the brand.

Disney's characters were as loved as ever. The stock fell because the cable bundle, which actually generated the cash, had started to shrink.

REEL11
SceneThe streaming bet
Years2016 → 2022

Buying the pipes, then the library

Disney had never had a direct relationship with its audience outside the parks. It had no emails and no viewing data. Iger nearly bought Twitter in 2016 (Jack Dorsey sat on Disney's board) and pulled out on a Sunday night before a Monday announcement. Instead, in August 2016 he bought a third of BAMTech, Major League Baseball's streaming technology arm, then took control in 2017–18. In 2017 Disney said it would pull its films from Netflix by 2019. Netflix was paying hundreds of millions a year, which Ben puts at about 2% of Disney's operating income.

Then the big one. In December 2017 Disney agreed to buy most of 21st Century Fox, the studio, its library and its international assets, for $52 billion in stock. Comcast bid too, and the price rose to $71.3 billion, which the hosts call a free $19 billion for Fox shareholders. After selling Fox's regional sports networks (~$14B) and the Sky stake (~$15B), the net cost was about $44 billion. It brought control of Hulu, the X-Men and Avatar, and an Indian business later merged into Reliance at a fraction of its price. The hosts rate it the worst of the big deals.

The deals, drawn to scale

Circle area is proportional to the headline price (nominal dollars). Hover or tap a circle.

Fox's headline price was larger than Cap Cities/ABC, Pixar, Marvel and Lucasfilm combined, and about 40% of Disney's value at the time.

Hosts' figures: Capital Cities/ABC $19B (1995); Pixar $7.4B (2006); Marvel ~$4B (2009); Lucasfilm ~$4B (2012); Fox $71.3B (2019), ~$44B net of divestitures (dashed ring). Not inflation-adjusted.

Disney+ was announced in April 2019 at $6.99 a month, and the stock rose 11% the next day. It launched in November 2019 with 10 million sign-ups in the first 24 hours. The five-year goal was 60–90 million subscribers. It passed 100 million in about 16 months, in March 2021, with the parks closed for COVID. That same month Disney's market cap peaked near $360 billion. The hosts give zero interest rates much of the credit.

Disney+ subscribers against the plan

Hosts' figures: 10M in 24 hours (Nov 2019); 26M after the first quarter; 100M announced March 2021; ~130M at the last report. The shaded band is the original 60–90M goal for year five. Points are milestones, not a continuous series.

The cracks were in the content. Iger handed the CEO job to Bob Chapek, the head of parks, in February 2020 and retired fully in December 2021. Lasseter was gone from Pixar, and Catmull had retired. Lucasfilm's sequel trilogy had no shared plan, and Solo flopped. Marvel had just finished its biggest story with Endgame, and was asked to raise output by about half to feed the service. Streaming loses its subscribers to churn constantly, and there's no home-video second window to recoup costs. Cumulative streaming losses reached about $13 billion.

D

David, quoting Ben from 2019Back in the original Disney+ episode, Ben warned that Disney might be underestimating how much content a streaming service consumes. The hosts call it firehose thinking, the opposite of a flywheel built on rare, best-in-class releases.

Chapek's tenure added self-inflicted wounds: a planned move of Imagineers to Florida that was cancelled after some had bought homes, a feud with Florida's governor, and a lavish Star Wars hotel that closed quickly. In November 2022, after an earnings call where investors hammered Disney+ losses, the board fired him and brought Iger back. The hosts' verdict is that Iger chose a peacetime caretaker for what was a wartime job.

Lesson 14Reel 11

Scarcity is part of the brand.

A flywheel runs on rare, beloved stories. A streaming service needs a constant stream of new ones. Feed the second with the first and both lose value.

REEL12
SceneIger again, and after
Years2022 → 2026

The parks carry the empire

Iger's second act was cleanup. The 2023 Hollywood strikes hit. Nelson Peltz's Trian, alongside the former Marvel chairman Ike Perlmutter, ran a costly proxy fight that went nowhere. In October 2023 ESPN began reporting as its own segment. In 2025 the NFL traded NFL Network and RedZone into ESPN for a 10% stake. At the end of 2025 ESPN launched direct to consumer at $30 a month, or $6 more bundled with Disney+ and Hulu. Bundles churn far less than single apps.

The parks drew about 145 million visits last year, still below the 157 million peak. Per-guest spending has risen about 5% a year for decades. In 2023 Disney said it would double park investment to about $60 billion over ten years, roughly half of it in Florida and Anaheim. The fleet grows from 8 cruise ships to 13, and a park in Abu Dhabi is in design. In February 2026 the board named Josh D'Amaro, head of parks and experiences, as CEO, effective in March, with Dana Walden as president and chief creative officer. Iger stays as an adviser through the end of 2026.

Disney today, by segment

Toggle between revenue and operating income. Watch which bar wins.

Hosts' rounded figures for the latest fiscal year: Entertainment ~$42B revenue / ~$4.7B operating income; Experiences ~$36B / ~$10B; Sports ~$18B / ~$3B. Company revenue ~$94B, net income ~$13B. Margins are calculated from these rounded numbers.

Lesson 15Reel 12

An experience that can't be cheapened holds its price.

Movies, TV and streaming can all be copied or commoditized. A trip to the park can't be made cheaper without making it worse, so it keeps its pricing power and now carries the company.

NOTESA
SceneAnalysis
FormatBen & David

Was Disney+ the right bet?

Doing nothing wasn't an option, the hosts agree. The alternatives were to merge with someone or shrink. Ben would have preferred a boutique Disney+ with only the great franchises, but concedes that a service like that can't survive the content treadmill. David's argument is that the theatrical system that used to introduce new stories to every generation has broken. Families don't go to theaters for a Ratatouille any more. Recent original Pixar films gross $200–400 million, and only sequels break records. Streaming is the only way left to reach every kid.

The scale gap

Netflix against Disney's streaming business, by the hosts' latest figures.

Hosts' figures. Netflix: ~325M subscribers last reported (Ben later says ~350M); ~$45B streaming revenue; ~$13.5B operating income. Disney: Disney+ ~130M (Hulu 64M, ESPN+ 24M); subscription revenue ~$22B (Ben) or ~$25B (David); ~$1B operating income. Disney stopped breaking streaming out after 2024.

Ben's new conclusion is that streaming rewards scale, so the winner looks like a kitchen sink, the way Netflix and the old cable bundle do, and Hulu fits that shape better than Disney+ does. The hosts note that Netflix's operating income alone is roughly equal to all of Disney's.

Bull and bear

Bear

The flywheel and the affiliate-fee machine are both damaged, maybe for good.

Ben's test: no major new franchise since about 2016 (Moana, Zootopia). Every big hit since has been harvested IP. Frozen may have been the last mega-hit.

Pixar, Marvel and Lucasfilm turned out to be twenty years of fuel, not fifty.

Bull

David: Disney's core characters are generational myths, like luxury brands. They fade and always come back.

Profit is near a record, and a 3–5% grower at this scale is fine.

There's more to buy. David pitches Bluey and Nintendo. Ben counters that Japan would never let Nintendo go.

Seven Powers

The hosts used Hamilton Helmer's framework only briefly, and only on the streaming business. Tap a card for their read.

Strength meters reflect the hosts' discussion, not a formal score. Powers they didn't discuss are marked so.

NOTESQ
SceneQuintessence
FormatTwo answers

The surplus, and the myth

Ben

The environment changed. From 1995 to 2019 profit came almost on autopilot: a cable bundle that raised its prices every year, plus theatrical hits followed by home-video windows. Now cable is shrinking, the box office is smaller, and streaming is expensive to build, to keep subscribers in, and to turn into events. That surplus was the anomaly, and Disney will be measured against it forever.

David

Disney is the home of generational myths, and that makes it close to unkillable. It moves in roughly twenty-year cycles. Peak Disney was the early 1990s and again the early 2010s. He wouldn't be surprised to see it back on top in about ten years.

Schematic, not data: a sketch of David's thesis. Peaks mark the eras the hosts named; the troughs follow the chapters above. The dashed curve is his guess, not a forecast.

Lesson 16Quintessence

Don't mistake a golden age for the baseline.

Cable on autopilot and home-video windows made 1995–2019 unusually easy. Leaders who come after a surplus have to be shrewder just to stand still.

END∞
SceneWhere they landed
As ofSummer 2026

Credits roll

Steve Jobs lived about five and a half years after the Pixar deal. At a last dinner with Iger he raised a glass to the two of them having saved two companies, which only makes sense once you see how fragile Pixar would have been without him. Eisner's twenty-one years are now remembered for ESPN as much as for the Renaissance. Katzenberg built DreamWorks into a rival. Iger, after two tenures and fifteen years of acquisitions, hands the company to the man who ran its parks. That choice says something on its own about where the value sits today.
